verses.1: The elder to Gaio the beloved, whom I love in truth.
verses.2: Beloved, I pray that all may go well with you and that you may be in good health, just as your soul is well.
verses.3: I have greatly rejoiced at the coming of the brothers, who have borne witness to your truth, just as you walk in truth.
verses.4: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.
verses.5: Beloved, you are doing what is faithful when you do something for the brothers, especially for strangers.
verses.6: These have testified about your love before the assembly, and you will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.
verses.7: For they went out for the sake of his name, taking nothing from the nations.
verses.8: We therefore ought to receive such people, so that we may become coworkers in the truth.
verses.9: I wrote something to the assembly, but the one who loves to have the first place among them, Diotrephes, does not accept us.
verses.10: Therefore, if I come, I will call to mind his deeds that he does, speaking evil and misleading us with his words; and not only does he himself refuse to receive the brothers, he also prevents those who want to and casts them out of the assembly.
verses.11: Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good comes from God; the one who does evil has not seen God.
verses.12: Demetrius is testified to by all, and by the truth itself. And we too testify, and you know that our testimony is true.
verses.13: I had many things to write to you, but I do not want to write them with ink and pen.
verses.14: But I hope to see you soon, and I will speak to you face to face.
verses.15: Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends individually by name.

notes:
Notes
- v. 1: "The elder" is a general title (πρεσβύτερος) used here rather than a specific name.  
- v. 9: "Diotrephes" is a name not found elsewhere in the New Testament.  
- v. 13: "With ink and pen" is a literal rendering of the Greek, which uses "black" (μέλανος) metaphorically for ink. The phrase emphasizes the physicality of writing rather than sending a letter.
